A prominent dressage trainer shot a belligerent student—and now maintains that he’s the real victim.

Until 2019, when he attempted to kill one of his students, Michael Barisone was a leading rider and trainer in the horse-handling sport of dressage. Today, he still owns a dressage farm in Loxahatchee, Florida, twenty miles inland from Palm Beach. This part of the state, drained by a grid of canals and centered on the village of Wellington, is the winter capital of America’s equestrian world. Barisone’s operation is relatively modest: there’s no high hedge, no entrance arch. On five acres, he has a stucco house that’s connected to a barn; white-fenced paddocks shaded by palms; and an outdoor riding ring. Along one end of the ring is a common neighborhood fixture: an eighty-foot-long mirror. Barisone, who’s in his early sixties, with a big Will Ferrell chin and a muscular build, can hold a conversation about his own good judgment, and the iniquity of his enemies, while riding a horse and monitoring his own reflection.

In dressage competitions, horses follow a short sequence of bouncing walks and trots, pirouettes and figures-of-eight. It’s an exhibition of control. A horse should do as it’s asked, in a way that projects noble interspecies harmony. Although dressage people have sometimes hoped to broaden their sport’s appeal by calling it “horse dancing,” that may create false expectations. In dressage’s usual form, one discrete movement follows another in a compulsory sequence. There may be a kind of flow, but there’s no sustained rhythm. Competitive dressage less resembles dancing than it does a D.M.V. road test—or floor exercises, if every gymnast had to do the same thing.

Barisone learned dressage during a middle-class childhood in far-upstate New York, and soon excelled at it. In the first of several meetings that I had with him last winter, in Loxahatchee and in New Jersey, he said that, given his ability, he “should have” competed in ten Olympic Games, going back to the eighties. It’s easy to sympathize with an athlete’s disappointments, but Barisone’s narrative of near-misses spans decades. He did represent the United States at the Beijing Olympics, in 2008, as the designated backup for a three-person team. He didn’t ride.

But when Barisone proposed to me that for twenty years he was the dressage equivalent of a major-league-baseball player, that seemed fair—with the caveats that there’s no league and no real audience. He competed at a high level; his income derived from selling horses he’d trained, and from coaching amateur dressage enthusiasts—his “ladies,” as he tends to call them—and their horses, along with a handful of Olympic-level professionals. Barisone and his former wife Vera Kessels followed the migration patterns of their people. They spent winters in Loxahatchee and summers at their other farm—since vacated—in western New Jersey. Barisone sat on dressage-world committees; he was, he told me, a “revered” member of the dressage community. In a 2012 episode of “The Colbert Report,” Stephen Colbert was shown riding in breeches and tails while Barisone, holding a whip, walked alongside him. Colbert’s horse was persuaded to piaffe—to trot in place, knees up, in a way that’s required in advanced dressage competitions. Barisone recently proposed that he was, at that moment, “the most famous horseman in the country.”

In Barisone’s Loxahatchee kitchen there is a dark-green safe the size of a vending machine. It used to stand in his office on the New Jersey farm. He has never seriously contested the idea that, on August 7, 2019, he took a handgun from the safe and drove a few hundred yards, to a house on his property where Lauren Kanarek, a thirty-eight-year-old student of his, was boarding with her boyfriend. He shot her twice.

“I did everything right, ” Barisone told me, a number of times, during long conversations held, over several days, at his kitchen table in Florida. His dominant tone was one of astonished resentment. He has the manner—and the abundance of files in Bankers Boxes—of someone struggling to correct a great miscarriage of justice. One could mistake him for an inmate preparing an appeal in a prison library. As we talked, I sometimes found it disorienting to remember that Barisone is a free man. His fiancée, Lara Osborne, usually joined us at the table; there were dogs and cats underfoot, in a sunny house with no mortgage and several pickup trucks out front. Now and then, a neigh carried through the kitchen’s French doors.

In 2022, Barisone was tried in New Jersey for attempted murder. He was found not guilty by reason of insanity. This was a remarkable verdict. Fewer than one per cent of Americans charged with felonies plead insanity, and the great majority of those who do have previously been hospitalized with a serious psychiatric condition. Barisone had no history of serious mental illness, and by the end of 2023 he had no such illness, according both to his own account and to the State of New Jersey.

This rare court-sanctioned narrative—sanity, criminal insanity, quick reversion to sanity—might seem like tremendous luck, given that he faced a decade or two in prison. But this isn’t how Barisone has experienced his freedom. It wasn’t surprising to hear him mourn what he’d lost since shooting someone in the chest twice. But it was striking to hear how fiercely he resented having lost anything at all. (He has lost time and money, and he can no longer compete in dressage.) “I want my dignity back,” he told me. “I want my reputation back.”

The first time I called him, he said, of the case, “You’re going to find it is a John Grisham novel combined with ‘Fatal Attraction’ combined with ‘Yellowstone.’ ” Barisone’s story has its evident hero, and its villain is Kanarek, his victim. In this presentation of events—a “scum of the earth” client, in his words, and a terrific guy who snapped, as anyone would have—Barisone has enjoyed near-universal support from the dressage community, and beyond. In much of the online discussion about the case, including in the forums of The Chronicle of the Horse , a long-established magazine, commenters have identified two victims, not one, and have almost always found Barisone’s victimhood the more compelling. A woman was shot, but a man was driven to shoot her, because she was annoying, and at times belligerent, in person and on social media. Kanarek has been widely scorned as a dressage interloper and as an embodiment of contemporary ills: a bullshitter, an entitled troll.

Barisone read me a note that he’d received after his acquittal, from a woman he didn’t know, who called Kanarek a “giant of wickedness.” The letter started, “Thank you for showing the rest of the world that good people can survive this kind of horrible torment and come out the winner.”

For Barisone, such regard isn’t enough. It doesn’t reset everything to how it was before he met Kanarek. “I will get to Trump,” he told me. “And I will get this undone. Watch me.” Since the shooting, Barisone has filed six lawsuits, and at least one more is being prepared. Last summer, about two years after a psychiatrist submitted to a court that Barisone bore “no ill will” toward Kanarek, Barisone filed a claim against the United States Equestrian Federation ( USEF ), for failing to punish her; it called her behavior “disgusting,” “abusive,” and “vulgar.” It also disparaged her riding ability and noted her acknowledged history of drug use. Barisone, meanwhile, was described as a man of substance; the document included his former financial assets and his dressage-competition results.

In Florida, Barisone imagined his vindication. He told me, “If this goes right—if I can make another team, a World Cup, a World Championship—I will be the biggest comeback story in the history of sports.”

On the day of the shooting, Kanarek was sitting alone on the porch outside the farmhouse where she was then living with Robert Goodwin, her boyfriend. The house was the first building that would be seen by a visitor to Barisone’s Hawthorne Hill Farm, in Morris County, New Jersey. A minute or so farther up a gravel road, just over a hill, stood a cluster of other buildings, where there was a clubroom, some bedrooms, horse stalls, and an indoor riding ring.

Kanarek, the eldest of three sisters, grew up in Livingston, a wealthy commuter town an hour’s drive east. In her late teens and twenties, she’d gone through what she described to me as “a bad patch of crazy things.” She didn’t finish college; her sisters began corporate careers in New York City. It’s clear that relations between Kanarek and her family had sometimes been strained, but her father, Jonathan Kanarek, a retired Wall Street equities trader, said in a recent call that there was never a rift. In a tone of disappointed acceptance, he brought up both her former drug-taking and a period, sometimes mentioned by Barisone and his allies, when she worked at a strip club. By 2016, Kanarek, who was then living in Greensboro, North Carolina, with Goodwin, a contractor, had revived a childhood enthusiasm for riding and taken up dressage. Jonathan called the sport “a great thing that led her out” of drugs. He and his wife, Kirby, helped out, both financially and by providing quotidian oversight, including of medical appointments.

In the spring of 2018, Lauren Kanarek paid for a month’s training at Barisone’s farm in Florida; she then began shuttling her two horses, seasonally, between his farms, as part of an arrangement that included lodging in New Jersey. In August, 2019, she and Goodwin were staying in the farmhouse’s second-floor apartment. It had its own ground-level entrance, which opened onto the porch; from there, steps led down to a concrete patio.

At about 2 P . M ., Barisone’s silver Ram truck appeared over the brow of the hill and pulled up by the patio. A few weeks earlier, relations between Barisone and Kanarek, which until then had been largely accommodating, and sometimes even playful, had suddenly turned fractious. They’d fallen out, in part over the care of her horses, but the dispute had skipped any intermediate stage of adult discord—say, pissily polite e-mails or form-letter threats of eviction. Each had begun working to destroy the other’s reputation. But this had been playing out largely at arm’s length, in the form of Facebook posts and duelling 911 calls. So Barisone’s appearance at the farmhouse unnerved Kanarek. In a recent conversation, she recalled feeling a rush of adrenaline. She went back indoors.

Goodwin was on the phone with a lawyer whom Kanarek had retained the previous day. He handed her his phone and went outside. Barisone, who Goodwin later said looked “sorrowful,” asked him, “How do we fix this? I don’t want a war.”

Goodwin said that they should let their lawyers handle things, and turned away. But Kanarek wanted to add that any resolution of their dispute had to include paying Goodwin for construction work he’d done on the farm, originally in a barter agreement. While she was still on the line with the lawyer, she approached Barisone.

In her memory, she and Barisone were standing just feet apart on the patio. Barisone is six feet three. Kanarek, who weighs about a hundred pounds, is five feet four. She had often taken a combative tone—in messages addressed to family members, or to old enemies, or to new ones she’d found among Trump supporters on Facebook. On this patio, a few weeks earlier, she’d had a pivotal confrontation with Barisone, arising out of a disagreement about horse feed. He’d loudly complained, and she’d also complained. In such situations, she told me, “I’m going to stand tall and yell back at you and take you by surprise.” (After the confrontation, she wrote to Goodwin and her father, “I said some pretty TRUE and fucked up things that literally silenced him for a full minute.”)

According to Kanarek and to the testimony of Edward David, the lawyer on the phone, there was no verbal combat this time. Kanarek told me that she hadn’t even begun to speak when Barisone drew a gun from somewhere.

“I didn’t even know it was a real gun,” Kanarek recalled to me. “I’m seeing that it’s pink—camouflage pink and black.” Perhaps it just shoots BBs, she thought. She remembered saying, “Oh, my God.” Barisone fired. “It was immediate— boom , boom ,” she told me. “It didn’t sound as loud as you would think.”

She dropped the phone. “I could see two complete holes in my shirt,” she told me. The holes were about two inches apart, above her left breast, near where a crocodile might be on a polo shirt. According to her account, Barisone then shot “at Rob’s head.” The bullet missed, and Goodwin retreated inside. Kanarek, laughing at her own description, recalled the “Superman moment” that followed: Goodwin seemed to fly back outside, horizontally. Goodwin is shorter than Barisone by about seven inches, but he also has a muscular build. He careened into Barisone and put him in a choke hold. During all this, one of the couple’s dogs yapped and bit at Barisone.

Kanarek told me that her bloody hands made it a struggle to call 911. When she got connected, she said, “I’ve been shot in the heart.”

On the recording of the 911 call, there’s a lot of barking, and some grunting from Goodwin, who says into the phone, “A man came here with a fucking gun. I’ve got him detained right now.” He also shouts, “Get that fucking dog inside now!” Goodwin has to be talking to Kanarek, which suggests that he hadn’t processed what had just happened. Kanarek hadn’t collapsed, and she could be hyperbolic when talking about ailments and injuries. (She’d recently written in a text that a spider bite had left her “150% incapacitated.”) But, as Kanarek tried to help debilitate Barisone by beating his head with a phone, Goodwin saw two exit holes in the back of her sweatshirt.

Kanarek recalled feeling dizziness, and pressure in her chest: “I’m, like, ‘How do I put a tourniquet on this wound that’s on my chest ?’ I was literally thinking, Do I have tampons?” She couldn’t breathe properly. It felt like “being in a pool and stuck under a raft that someone was on.”

The line to the 911 dispatcher was still open when, after about five minutes, a police officer, Derek Heymer, arrived at the farmhouse. Kanarek, who remained conscious, told him, “I’m shot—please help me.”

Other officers arrived, and Kanarek was treated with chest seals. Barisone, handcuffed, began to say, “I had a good life,” to no one in particular. The judge at his first hearing detected in this statement a fatalism that made him a possible continuing threat to himself and others—although the refrain could also have been interpreted as an expression of affront. Later that afternoon, Barisone, while being treated for a broken arm and other injuries at a local hospital, complained, “They destroyed my life.”

In an emergency operation in the same hospital, doctors opened up Kanarek’s chest. They clamped her aorta, to keep her alive—she’d lost about half the blood in her body—before repairing her lungs. Today, Barisone claims to have no memory of the time between being in his office up the hill and waking, the next day, with one arm shackled to a hospital bed.

“Dèy,” “Etna,” “Are They Dead Yet?,” and “Unbelonging.”

Dèy , by Edwidge Danticat (Knopf) . Set among Haitian Americans in Miami, this novel centers on Magnolia, a young mother who is at a mall when a mass shooter opens fire. She escapes and, because she does not want to be defined by the tragedy, decides not to tell anyone about it. In the weeks that follow, Magnolia plans her daughter’s birthday, negotiates her relationship with her daughter’s father, and coördinates medical care for her aging parents, who are living in Haiti amid growing violence. This fascinatingly banal aftermath forces the reader to confront the normalcy of such horror in a world where approximately seven per cent of American adults have been at the scene of a mass shooting. Danticat asks, Is gun violence newsworthy anymore? Or is it everyday life?

Etna , by Paul Yoon (Scribner) . This novel’s narrator is a dog who lives on a farm in a nameless country that is descending into war. One day, a woman arrives who can speak with him telepathically; she names him Etna and takes him to be trained by American soldiers as a combat dog. After years of conflict, Etna is a grizzled veteran who knows how to search for explosives and how to kill. But, when the war ends, the world as he knew it has been destroyed. He abandons his handlers and wanders the wasted land, searching for any home that might be left. Yoon’s choice to plant his sparely written novel in a canine perspective reveals the devastation that human aggression can inflict on all creatures.

Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.

Are They Dead Yet? , by Sam Roberts (Bloomsbury) . “Writing obituaries is not a job for the faint of heart, nor the heartless,” Roberts announces early in this pithy and engaging survey of what he calls “the dead beat.” Roberts, who has written more than sixteen hundred obituaries, retraces the origins of the form (in ancient Rome) and the emergence of the modern newspaper obituary (in the eighteenth century). As he describes the process by which writers and editors decide who among the “more than 150,000 or so people who die each day around the world qualify to be immortalized in the Times ,” he demonstrates how and why obituaries “demand a degree of empathy not required of, say, political reporting or restaurant reviews.”

Unbelonging , by Catherine Jagoe (Wisconsin) . This sensitively observed essay collection, by a translator of Spanish literature, considers the elusive nature of home. “Defining home, identifying a homeland, feeling at home. I just can’t seem to manage it,” Jagoe writes. In trying, however, she ranges elegantly across experiences, from the ecstasy of swimming to the “deep, dark wintering” of depression. The act of patiently noticing the physical world runs through the book. In Madrid, she reëncounters the “upland light, landscape, and air” of Nigeria, where she lived as a small child; and though southern Wisconsin, where she lives today, lacks the “transparent, haunting fragrance” of wild bluebells in the woods of England, her country of birth, she discovers a place for herself there nonetheless, through close engagement with the landscape.

America’s everywhere millionaires built fortunes from hot dogs, car dealerships, medical practices, and convenience stores. Then they learned how to protect them.

Billionaires have never been more central to the cultural and political conversation, more impressed with themselves, or more consumed with a sense of their own victimhood. From “Billions” and “Succession” to the latest social-media spasms of Musk or Ackman or Arnault, billionaires offer a grim and garish spectacle from which it’s hard to look away, and, let’s admit it, we often don’t. That’s understandable: there are more of them, and they’re richer than ever. In 2025, to get onto the Forbes list of the top four hundred American billionaires, you needed a cool $3.8 billion. The average wealth of that group was $16.5 billion, and their collective net worth was $6.6 trillion. There were another five hundred American billionaires who didn’t even make the list.

This is an unprecedented concentration of wealth and power among the super-rich. When we talk about wealth, we mainly talk about billionaires. But what if that’s not the most important truth about wealth in America? What if there were another group that, without drawing much attention, had grown collectively thirteen times richer than the Forbes 400? And that was even more effective at using its financial-political clout? And what if a typical member of that class looked less like Logan Roy and more like this:

He tells them, when they buy a Toyota, they’re turning their dollars into yen. And they believe him. A hundred twelve units new and used moved in the first five months of 1979, with eight Corollas, five Coronas including a Luxury Edition Wagon, and that Celica that Charlie said looked like a Pimpmobile unloaded in these first three weeks of June already, at an average gross mark-up of eight hundred dollars per sale. Rabbit is rich.

It was percipient of John Updike to latch on to the car dealership as the foundation of Harry (Rabbit) Angstrom’s Everyman prosperity in his tetralogy of novels. As Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick show in their brilliant new study, “The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There” (Holt), the car dealer—Rabbit, or Buddy Garrity in “Friday Night Lights,” or Daniel LaRusso, the grownup Karate Kid, in “Cobra Kai”—is a true archetype of American wealth. Car dealer, beer-distribution magnate, partner in a medical practice or a law firm: these ordinary, ubiquitous business owners represent a collective prosperity at least as consequential as the ascendancy of the billionaire, only much less conspicuous. “In a sense,” Zidar and Zwick argue, “Main Street Millionaires are hiding in plain sight. The supermarket where you shop, the restaurant where you order a burger, and the convenience store where you buy gas, newspapers, and coffee may all be parts of huge chains that have made their founders very rich.”

Zidar and Zwick got onto this story through their work for the Treasury at the Office of Tax Analysis, which studies the impact of tax legislation, actual and prospective. The two young economists, from Berkeley and Harvard, respectively, were assigned the task of finding out how much tax business owners pay. That might sound straightforward—might, indeed, sound like the kind of thing the government should already know—but the tax code is complicated, and the I.R.S.’s various databases are thoroughly siloed and anonymized. To answer the question, they and another colleague set about finding who owned businesses, connecting those business records with individual taxpayers. It was a complicated process involving years of work, and they more than earned the endearingly nerdy, self-appointed nickname the Tax Ninjas. They discovered what comes close to being a new class in America, the “everywhere millionaire” of their title. There are a lot of them: nearly five million households with a net worth of at least five million dollars; more than two million decamillionaires, worth at least ten million; and around sixty-five thousand centimillionaires, worth a hundred million and up. The sheer mass of these numbers means that, in Zidar and Zwick’s words, in contemporary America, for all the fuss around billionaires, “these are the real rich.”

For an explanation of how they got that way, we need a brief detour into the tax code. The modern federal income tax, authorized by a constitutional amendment in 1913, began with a top rate of seven per cent and was dramatically expanded to help finance the First World War. Its top rate later rose from twenty-five per cent, in 1925, to ninety-four per cent, during the Second World War. Corporation tax, introduced in 1909, followed a similar trajectory, peaking at fifty-three per cent in 1968. By the time Ronald Reagan became President, in 1981, the top rates of income and corporation tax stood at seventy and forty-six per cent, respectively.

Republicans in Congress wanted to cut taxes, and Democrats wanted to simplify the tax code. The outcome was the bipartisan Tax Reform Act of 1986, which did both. In the process, the bill introduced a novelty in American history by leaving the top rate of corporation tax, thirty-four per cent, higher than the top rate of federal income tax, twenty-eight per cent. At the same time, the bill boosted the allure of a special-enterprise category: the “pass-through,” in which a business passes its net income through to the tax returns of individual owners, who pay the lower individual rate of tax, rather than the higher corporate rate, while avoiding dividend taxes. One bookkeeping expert quoted by Zidar and Zwick calls owning a small business “the best tax deal in America.”

That is who the everywhere millionaires are: owners of pass-through businesses. These businesses are everywhere, and they do pretty much everything. Our image of wealth skews glamorous and coastal. These businesses and their owners don’t. Some of the firms are well known, part of the familiar roadside furniture of American life—Buc-ee’s, Bass Pro Shops. There are many, many more, and the catalogue of what they do and where they do it is a Whitmanian portrait of capitalism: the “world’s largest mozzarella maker,” Texas’s largest supplier of seamless gutters, “the biggest in the world in the high-end skiwear market,” gas-and-convenience-megastore tycoons, a “massive family-owned supplier of door handles,” “a company that just stored documents for medical and financial firms,” makers of car parts, bakers of hamburger buns, distributors of toilet paper, a tanning-bed mogul who pivoted to waxing when she realized that tanning was going out of fashion.

As for what the people who own these businesses are like, Zidar and Zwick give both a statistical summary and individual portraits. Statistically, the mean pass-through decamillionaire is a white, college-educated, sixty-two-year-old man—older than one might expect, because these businesses take a while to build. (He’s also unusually likely to be married: the average for the general population is around fifty per cent, but among this cohort it is ninety.) We all know people who are laid-back, curious about lots of different things, and have a good work-life balance. These small-business owners are not like that. They tend toward monomania. Their days are, in Zidar and Zwick’s words, “full, busy, and mundane.” They usually own only one business, and they dedicate themselves to it unrelentingly, with few outside interests or hobbies, a high tolerance for risk, and little appetite for work-life balance. (Rabbit Angstrom wasn’t like that, but Rabbit Angstrom didn’t stay rich.)

The portraits in “The Everywhere Millionaire” are vivid. In 1976, Nancy Mueller’s young children were enrolled in school in California, and she was on her way to play tennis when she stopped and asked herself where she wanted to be in a decade: to be better at tennis, or to be doing something else? “I wanted to have something to show for the next ten years,” she recalled. “I wanted to make it count.” She went into business making frozen miniature quiches, “leasing space from a dilapidated empanada factory that was vacant while the owner served time in jail.” Mueller adapted a washing machine to take water out of spinach and had her production equipment improved by an aerospace engineer who had left the industry in protest of the Vietnam War; soon, she was making a hundred thousand mini quiches a day. What she wasn’t making yet was profit—“you’re shipping dollar bills with every case of quiche,” her accountant father told her. Her big break came in 1983, when Price Club placed a large order, followed by other warehouse stores. By the late nineteen-nineties, she had an eighty-six-thousand-square-foot production facility and was making fifty million dollars in sales, seemingly undeterred by the tragic loss of her husband to suicide in 1994. At one point, she said, the business earned an eighteen-per-cent pre-tax profit margin. Worried that the warehouse stores would suddenly drop her products one day, as they are known to do, she sold the business to a leveraged-buyout firm in 1999 and retired, in Zidar and Zwick’s words, to “sail off into the sunset,” aboard her superyacht, the Andiamo.

A different energy attaches to the story of another pass-through business owner, Dick Portillo. He grew up poor, in a rough Chicago housing project, and joined the Marines in 1957, seven days after graduating from high school. He liked fighting. On his first date with his future wife, “he took her to a lake but told her that he had to participate in a rumble there.” In 1963, with a family to support, exhausted and injured from manual labor, he decided, “I had to figure something out. I had to create a future for us.” Portillo thought he had spotted something: Chicago was famous for hot dogs, but its suburbs were short of places to buy them. He opened his first hot-dog stand in a discount-store parking lot in a homemade six-by-twelve trailer.

Many adventures later, Portillo sold his business to private equity, his chain of thirty-eight restaurants and two commissaries valued at a cool billion. (He came to regret it. Portillo was bored by retirement.) The valuation reflected an astonishing fact: where a successful McDonald’s could have a turnover of three million dollars a year, a Portillo’s could turn over nine million. We get a glimpse of how Portillo’s got so successful in the story of how he fended off competition from a rival, Ditka Dogs, set up by the beloved local figure Mike Ditka, the head coach of the Chicago Bears. According to Portillo, Ditka’s team had poached one of his managers. A few days before the restaurant was due to open, Portillo invited the manager to see him. “I told him that he did what every man, every leader of the house, every bread-winner would do.” Portillo began taking money out of his pockets and putting it on the table in front of him. “There was about $12,000 on the table now. I told him it was all his if he did one more thing.” Ditka’s new restaurant was opening on Saturday. The “one more thing”—in addition to coming back to Portillo’s for higher pay and convincing the other employees who had been hired away to do the same—was to quit on Friday. “Portillo attended the grand opening and sat with a cup of coffee to watch the mess unfold.” The reason you’ve never been to a branch of Ditka Dogs is that the company no longer exists. The name of Portillo’s yacht? Top Dog.

The common thread in “The Everywhere Millionaire” is not dazzling innovation. Anyone might have thought to make a fortune from quiche, or hot dogs, or human-resource management, or office supplies, or convenience stores, or gas stations. The secret ingredient is no secret: it’s the sheer remorselessness, ingenuity, and resilience of the business owners.

If that were all there was to the everywhere-millionaire story, we could celebrate it as an example of how non-crony capitalism is supposed to work, a meritocratic free-for-all. Unfortunately, there is a shadow side. As Zidar and Zwick argue, their protagonists, for all their virtues, are also “central characters in the saga of rising inequality.” Between 1980 and 2024, the share of national income going to American workers is estimated to have declined from sixty-five per cent to fifty-six per cent, meaning that “nine cents of every dollar that a firm creates that used to go to workers now goes to firm owners.” There have been increases in productivity, remarkable ones. The authors, surveying “top-owned firms,” report a recent rise in labor productivity from thirty-four thousand dollars a year to fifty-two thousand dollars a year. If the annual proceeds had been shared equally, that eighteen-thousand-dollar increase would have meant nine thousand dollars each. Instead, fifteen thousand dollars has gone to owners and three thousand dollars to workers. The so-called Gilded Age and the years following saw huge income disparities; in the early twentieth century, the highest-earning one per cent of households earned eighteen per cent of all income, and the bottom ninety per cent earned sixty per cent. The equivalent numbers in 2022 are worse: twenty per cent and around fifty per cent.

Social mobility has also declined. Poor children born in 1940 had about a ninety per cent chance of earning more than their parents. The chance for those children born in 1980 was closer to seventy per cent. According to a 2014 analysis, the chance of moving from the bottom fifth to the top fifth of earners was 7.5 per cent. Turn this around, and it means that if you were born in that bottom fifth, you could be 92.5 per cent sure that you wouldn’t get to the top fifth. “The chance of making it to the top as a poor kid in the twenty-first century is about half of what it was at the beginning of the twentieth,” Zidar and Zwick write. That means that the richest and most powerful country in the world has seen a dramatic and dispiriting decline in opportunity for the less well off.

The link between inequality and the everywhere millionaire runs through politics. Entrepreneurship is important for upward economic mobility: nine per cent of those who made the transition from the bottom fifth to the top fifth are entrepreneurs; only 1.3 per cent attended élite universities. But that rise is harder than it used to be. The pass-through owners are very active in politics, both at the federal level—where decamillionaires hold twelve per cent of congressional seats, despite representing less than one per cent of the U.S. population—and at the state level, which, Zidar and Zwick point out, is another huge focus of lobbying money. A consistent theme in their political activity has been to pull up the drawbridge and make it harder for new entrepreneurs to get rich in the same ways.

The free-market economy of the U.S. has, when you look closely, a remarkable number of restrictive practices, many of them concentrated in industries where the Main Street Millionaires got rich. Beer distribution—the highly lucrative and highly protected intermediary industry between brewers and bars—is one. Car dealerships are another. In both cases, legal protections designed to defend the little guy against bullies—the brewers, the car manufacturers—ended up creating a new category of bully. Burns—the director of “New York: A Documentary Film”—had had a run-in with a metal paper-towel holder, to the tune of seven stitches. “Geysers of blood,” he said, entering a shadowy editing booth. “I got a photo if you want.”

Burns, the younger brother of fellow-filmmaker Ken Burns, was in the midst of making other bloody cuts: editing two long-gestating new episodes of “New York,” set to air later this month on PBS. One of his editors, Parker Dixon, sat at a console, staring at an iMac screen. The two began to work, Burns thinking aloud, Dixon cuing up footage. “Ric puts pen to paper,” Dixon said. “And from there we just feel it forward.”

Burns nodded. “It’s a funny balance,” he said. “Sometimes you want to be seeing what you hear, but a whole lot of times you don’t.”

Burns has worked out of the same offices overlooking Broadway and Seventy-third Street since 1989, two years before he and a collaborator, James Sanders, began work on “New York.” The first seven episodes, fourteen hours in all, aired between 1999 and 2001, covering everything from Henry Hudson’s first sail up the harbor to the city’s near-bankruptcy in the nineteen-seventies. Jackson, the feminist writer Carmen Boullosa, and the Times culture critic Wesley Morris. Godwits make the longest non-stop migration in the bird world. That might be the least of their marvels. Can they survive a changing planet?

On a sunny June morning, in a bog outside Beluga, Alaska, I met a Hudsonian godwit. She had inky eyes and a long, slightly upturned beak that was pinkish-orange at its base and brownish-black at its tip. The feathers on her back were of mottled sepia tones, and those on her belly were rusty brown and painterly white. Her legs reminded me of the slender inserts of spring-loaded ballpoint pens, and her feet were refined pterodactyl claws. Her name (among humans) was A34, and she was about the size of a city pigeon. She was in the hands of Nathan Senner, a conservation biologist, who removed and replaced her geotag; measured her head, beak, wing, and leg; weighed her; and took two tail feathers and a sample of her blood. From that small number of data points, he can deduce where she’s been, how her feathers have grown, what genetic subgroup she belongs to, and her degree of exposure to mercury.

Senner leads a research laboratory at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, that is largely focussed on how migratory shorebirds, such as godwits, respond to environmental change. He grew up in Anchorage, where school loudspeakers announced the street corners on which moose had been sighted. In high school, he wrote an occasional “Birding with Nathan” column for the Anchorage Daily News . Senner’s father, Stanley, has devoted more than five decades to the conservation of migratory shorebirds. Starting in the nineteen-seventies, Stanley and his colleagues have been sounding the alarm on the vulnerability of shorebirds and working to protect key habitats, such as Alaska’s Copper River Delta. “Back then, no one was even talking about climate change,” he told me recently. Since 1980, roughly half of migratory shorebird species’ populations have declined by more than fifty per cent.

Migratory shorebirds are usually not a person’s first bird crush. They lack the supernatural aura of the resplendent quetzal, and they don’t go in for outlandish mating displays like that of the prairie chicken. As the Princeton University biology professor and shorebird-lover David Wilcove put it, migratory shorebirds can give an impression of being “little brown guys, buzzing around in the mud, not too big and not too small, and, whether one is a stint or a phalarope or a knot or a godwit, they’re just kind of there.” And yet, Wilcove told me, they are a birder’s kind of bird. Once people get to know them, they tend to fall in love.

Relatively few people have laid eyes on Hudsonian godwits. The birds mostly divide their time between remote northern bogs and muddy South American shores. John James Audubon apparently never saw a living one; he based his drawing of them in “Birds of America” on a few specimens he found in markets. Arthur Cleveland Bent, in a 1927 installment of his twenty-one-volume series, “Life Histories of North American Birds,” wrote of Hudsonian godwits, “I can count on the fingers of one hand the red-letter days when I have been privileged to see this rare and handsome wader.”

It’s entirely possible that I had encountered A34 two months before seeing her in Alaska. In March, I had travelled from New York to Chiloé Island, in Chilean Patagonia. Flocks of Hudsonian godwits (the smallest of the four godwit species and the least well known) spend from roughly early October to April in and around the tidal mudflats there. The island also has Humboldt penguins, giant rhubarb plants with leaves as large as umbrellas, and the world’s smallest species of deer. Castro, the main town, is famous for its brightly painted wooden seaside houses, which rest on tall stilts to accommodate the tide. Homo sapiens is a shore-loving species. About forty per cent of us live within sixty miles of a coast.

Chiloé is where Hudsonian godwits spend their non-breeding season and express their non-breeding personality, which is intensely gregarious and food-oriented. If you walk at low tide on the mudflats of Pullao Bay, you will see godwits bobbing for bivalves and worms, dunking their beaks in and out of the ground as if they were darning. They share their feasting grounds with oystercatchers, ducks, whimbrels, greater yellowlegs and lesser yellowlegs, and other shorebirds that neither I nor my Merlin Bird ID app could identify. The longer I watched the shorebirds on Chiloé Island, the stronger my impression was that they were dressed for a masquerade or a carnival, with some wearing stout beaks, some slim ones, others elegantly curved ones. The pale bellies and darker backs of many of the birds made it look as if they had on fashionable capes over slender, hosiery-clad legs. They called out to one another and occasionally broke into cotillion-like flight. The Hudsonian godwits appeared eternally committed to these revels. There was no sign that they were about to fly nearly ten thousand miles to Alaska, a wondrous and mystifying migration that one scientist called “technically impossible.”

Birds are in trouble. Migratory shorebirds are in especially bad trouble. And long-distance migratory shorebirds, like the Hudsonian godwit, may be in the most trouble. “Birds are sentinels,” Stanley Senner told me. “The ecosystems they rely on are ecosystems we rely on as well, though it can take time to convince people of that.” Studies show that, without shorebirds, coastlines erode more quickly, trap less carbon, and are more likely to become unbalanced. In the Yellow Sea, for example, shorebirds feed on crabs whose population needs to be kept in check, as they graze on native vegetation. In some ways, shorebirds are analogous to the wolves that hunt the deer and elk populations that eat the tree saplings that become the trees that beavers use to build dams that help the fish—and so on. Shorebirds also transport and disperse essential seeds and nutrients. Our interests align, as they say. Also, like all birds, they are lovable, alien, awesome, and alive. Not long ago, I saw a dead magpie on a country highway. Other magpies gathered around it, as if saddened and confused. When a car approached, they scattered. After the car passed, they returned to their fallen friend. So there’s also that.

To protect birds effectively, we need to understand them. So much about godwits remains unknown, including where and when they encounter their most mortal threats. Since their epic migration is maybe their most difficult-to-fathom characteristic, we may as well start there.

The story of bird migration, as narrated in Western civilization, often begins with Aristotle, who wrote that, in the winter, redstarts turn into robins and garden warblers turn into blackcaps. This sounds silly but, compared with the idea that a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, it seems reasonable. Olaus Magnus, a sixteenth-century Swedish priest, argued that barn swallows disappear in the fall because they hibernate at the bottom of ponds. That also seems absurd until you learn about the common poorwill, which resembles an old piece of bark and spends months of winter nestled almost imperceptibly in the crevices of logs or among piles of rocks. This wasn’t scientifically documented until 1948, although the poorwill has long been known to the Hopi as hölchoko , “the sleeping one.”

The Maori tell a story about how a godwit showed their ancestors the way from their ancient homeland of Hawaiki to New Zealand, more than a thousand miles away. But, to most people, avian migrations of that length were long unimaginable. In 1822, a hunter near the German town of Klütz shot down a stork; when he collected the bird, he saw that it had a wooden spear through its neck, later determined to be of African origin. Hunters eventually found more such Pfeilstorchs (arrow storks), giving credence to the hypothesis that the white stork not only migrated but did so between Europe and Africa. In some ways, this was a downgrade: the seventeenth-century minister Charles Morton, who wrote a popular physics textbook, claimed that birds migrated to the moon. He supposed that they fuelled a sixty-day flight there with body fat (reasonable) and that the journey was made easier by the minimal atmospheric resistance in space (also reasonable).

Migratory birds in captivity develop Zugunruhe, an agitated fitfulness, at certain times of year. Scientists don’t know precisely what provoked A34 to set off northward one spring afternoon, with a flock of her fellows, though, if they did, they might better know how her species will be affected by the shifting seasons of our changing climate. Godwits cannot soar like hawks or glide like albatrosses. They migrate by continuously flapping their wings. They must navigate crosswinds and headwinds, storms and maybe an occasional hurricane, continuing on day after day, night after night. As best as we can tell, they do not, while flying, eat or drink or sleep (at least not with more than one hemisphere of their brain at a time). After a journey of hundreds of hours and thousands of miles, they descend on a snow-covered shore at the Cook Inlet of southern Alaska or another favored breeding ground. They land considerably lighter than when they took off. “Many arriving shorebirds seem to be tired,” the ornithologist and conservationist Joseph Archibald Hagar wrote, in his foundational monograph, “Nesting of the Hudsonian Godwit at Churchill, Manitoba,” from 1966. In a field-diary entry, Hagar describes a group of birds that “within a minute or two dropped into some sunny spot out of the wind, tucked heads into scapulars, and went to sleep, not to move again for as long as we watched.”

In 1976, the young ornithologist Robert Gill took a job with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in Anchorage. He was dispatched to the Alaska Peninsula to do biological inventories on public land that was up for lease to private companies. During those long-lit Alaskan summer days, walking across salt marshes and through the foothills of the mountains, Gill encountered thousands upon thousands of migratory shorebirds. He told me, “In Alaska, where the seasons are so prominent, it’s very dramatic. It feels like all the birds turn up over the course of one weekend in May.” Along with godwits, the peninsula was a summer home to yellowlegs, dowitchers, sandpipers, Arctic terns, and other species. But almost no one was aware that so many birds relied on this land. How the birds managed their journeys, where they might stop along the way, even how many of them there were—no one knew for sure. “In the vast expanses of wetlands and coastal tundra, you could see why,” Gill said.

The extinction of the once common passenger pigeon, famously described by the naturalist John Muir in his memoir (“I have seen flocks streaming south in the fall so large that they were flowing over from horizon to horizon in an almost continuous stream all day long, at the rate of forty or fifty miles an hour, like a mighty river in the sky”), was part of the impetus behind the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Godwits are protected under the act, so killing them or holding them captive, even for scientific purposes, is highly regulated. Also, they’re difficult to capture. Gill’s means of learning more about them was limited, he said, to “the kind of observational work done by old-school naturalists.”

In October of 1987, Gill received a call about nine bar-tailed godwits that had crashed into a radar dome near Cold Bay, Alaska, and died. “They were greaseballs,” he recalled. “They made any Christmas goose look lean.” The carcasses were sent to a lab to be analyzed. Fifty-five per cent of their body mass turned out to be fat. Gill suspected that these chubby godwits were preparing to fly non-stop from Alaska to New Zealand, where this species wintered. However, at that time, the longest known non-stop migration flight was barely half that long. “But, if they were going to stop in French Polynesia, why carry all that baggage?” Gill reasoned.

The lab also measured the birds’ internal organs. Gill’s collaborator, Theunis Piersma, noticed something peculiar: the guts, gizzard, liver, and kidneys of these birds were very small—it was like cutting open a lion and encountering digestive organs the size of a house cat’s. Then, in March of 1992, some forty godwit carcasses were seized from a poacher in New Zealand. These were birds in a very different part of their migratory cycle, and their digestive organs, when analyzed, were of more normal proportions. In 1998, Piersma and Gill published their findings in a paper titled “Guts Don’t Fly: Small Digestive Organs in Obese Bar-Tailed Godwits,” concluding that the birds shrank their digestive organs to reduce their weight and their metabolic demands during a non-stop migration. And then, somehow, regrew them.

This conclusion remained debatable. For one thing, Gill and Piersma had no direct evidence that the birds flew without stopping. At the time, there were no tags sufficiently lightweight for tracking birds as small as godwits. But transmitters kept shrinking, and, in 2007, Gill flew to New Zealand, where, after a lot of patient, muddy field work, he succeeded in putting tags on sixteen bar-tailed godwits. The trackers could send signals to satellites to pinpoint the birds’ location. By today’s norms, the trackers were pretty heavy. Many of them failed within months, but one lasted much longer than expected.

A female godwit, E7, took off on March 17, 2007, from near the Piako River, on New Zealand’s North Island. She flew more than six thousand miles non-stop to a nature preserve on the Yalu River, near the China-North Korea border; she stayed there for a little more than a month; she arrived at her nesting area in Alaska on May 15th and spent the summer there. The tracker was still working on August 29th, when E7 started flying southeast, over the Pacific. Gill’s team was doing field work in western Alaska and had only spotty internet service; the team would gather around a laptop, waiting for the updates on E7’s location to come through. North of Kauai, she took a slight right turn and continued flying. On September 7th, after more than two hundred hours aloft, she landed at the mouth of the Piako River, back on the North Island of New Zealand, where Gill had first met her.

Before E7, the longest documented non-stop migratory-bird flight was that of a Far Eastern curlew who had flown about four thousand miles. E7 flew some seven thousand without a break. The flight defied reason. “I had an engineering professor at M.I.T. call me up and say he gave his students an assignment to compare the size and flight range of E7 to a 747 jet,” Gill said.

How all the stories begin. A large hand lowered, your small hand lifted.

Rainwater in puddles on the garage floor. Slow-drifting fog, mist.

The smell of her father’s breath, like fumes.

In the back seat of the car, a potted plant, its blooms wrapped in crinkly cellophane, amid random newspapers, napkins, coffee cups. Also, a small suitcase so stuffed that one of the compartments was only partly zipped.

C’mon, silly. Nothing to be afraid of.

Kit smiled uncertainly. For Daddy was smiling. Nothing to be afraid of ? It had not occurred to Kit that there might be something to be afraid of.

Two elevators in the parking garage. Both were slow to ascend to the top level. Daddy took the concrete steps down, gripping Kit’s hand.

Kit was out of breath descending the stairs.

But here was relief: in the cold, wet air, she could not smell Daddy’s strong breath. And Daddy stood tall above her and would protect her, for he was the daddy, as he told Kit often.

He remarked, as they approached the revolving doors of the tall building, on how “cavernous” this place was, which, he said, laughing, could sound to the careless ear like “carnivorous.”

Kit had no idea what her father meant, these jokes of his. Though, now that they were together so much, she heard them often.

Nothing to be afraid of, smoochie! Hauling Kit into the revolving door the way you’d lift a startled little dog, for, Daddy knew, Kit was afraid of revolving doors that moved too fast for her short legs.

See? Nothing to be afraid of.

Inside the hospital, a high ceiling, bright lights, and echoing voices. That sharp smell, a chemical smell, that made Kit’s nostrils pinch and caused a sick sensation in her stomach, for, she remembered, she’d been here before, in this hospital place.

It almost returned to Kit then—what this place was, and who was waiting for them inside. But then the memory faded the way a dream does when you open your eyes too soon.

Sir ? Excuse me. . . .

Long-legged Daddy walking fast but not fast enough, for he was stopped by a security guard and asked to show I.D. He extracted his driver’s license from his wallet, saying, in a loud, sarcastic voice, Every fucking time pretending you don’t know who the fuck I am!

Embarrassing to Kit, Daddy’s loud voice. Strangers glancing at him, curious, startled.

Usually, Kit’s father was affably smiling. People liked him on sight or wanted to like him, women especially. A man who, if he smiled, winked. Even sarcasm turned sweet in his mouth.

Kit’s father scrawled his name, or an insolent semblance of his name, into a book. The security guard issued him a time-stamped badge. Waved Kit’s father through the checkpoint stiff-faced, unsmiling.

But a smile for her, sweet little girl tugged along by Daddy.

More walking. More jostling. Behind Kit’s eyes, tiredness swam like a soft explosion of warm water.

Almost Kit’s bedtime, except there was no bedtime now, exactly.

For the day had been long. Kit could not remember the beginning of this long day.

Driving to the bank. It was impressive to Kit, to drive with Daddy to the bank.

Kit’s father expressed the wish for cash. Good old-fashioned cash. In polite-Daddy voice, expressed the wish to close out the account.

But there was a problem—a bank officer had to be summoned.

Your wife’s signature is required to close out the account.

Kit steeled herself, knowing that, since the bank officer was a woman, there would be a disagreement, because Kit’s father did not like to be “bossed around” by a woman.

Kit’s father’s voice rising, indignant. He sent Kit away to sit in a chair by the wall.

Eventually, a second bank officer was summoned. This was a man, an older man with a waffle face and a thatch of white hair atop a burly body, but he was a man, so Kit was not so worried.

In the hard-cushioned chair, Kit could not keep her eyes open, and being asleep and being awake became confused.

Roughly, Daddy woke Kit, tugged her to her feet, asking if she needed to use the rest room now. Better now than later.

What was the right answer? If Kit said no, she would be scolded for changing her mind later, for when Kit needed a bathroom it was often sudden, a near-emergency.

But, if Kit said yes, maybe that was a wrong answer, too, for Daddy was rattling his car keys. She could see that he was in a hurry.

Daddy’s eyes squinched when he smiled. Winking, assuring Kit that they were in the homestretch now.

The words “ ho-o-ome streh-h-h-tch ” were drawn out like an elastic band.

No idea what any of this meant, but Kit laughed to please Daddy.

Lunch they’d eaten late, in the car. Out of crinkly white paper bags. Daddy drinking from a can of something harsh-smelling, then from a bottle of something sweet-smelling inside another paper bag. Kit was very hungry, but then not so hungry. Coarse hamburger meat she had to chew and chew. Icy-cold French fries smeared with ketchup, falling between the front seats, where even Kit’s small hand could not retrieve them.

Hey! Wake up! Kit’s father sounded more amused than annoyed.

Kit’s eyes flew open. There’d been Kit’s mother smiling at Kit, trying to explain, but her words were muffled. Trying to explain why she’d gone away, how it was not her choice but just something that had happened.

Kit did not like elevators.

Daddy always positioned himself right in front of the elevator door. With Kit in front of him, his hands heavy on her shoulders.

But, when the elevator door opened, people pushed out. Kit’s father seemed never to be prepared for people pushing out, as if it were a personal annoyance to him.

Nudging Kit. Get in! Push in!

Always too many people. Adult legs, handbags pressing against Kit. Close, stale air that Kit tried not to breathe.

And, if you were the first into the elevator, that meant you were pushed toward the back as people stepped in, and always there were more people pushing in than there was room for, and so a man’s voice would intervene sharply, No more room! Take the next elevator, please .

The elevator door shut. Lights began to flicker on a panel above the door, indicating the floors—1, 2, 3. . . . Kit tried not to panic. As the elevator was rising, she knew, the cable pulling it up could snap at any time; suddenly, the elevator could be falling.

Once, Kit had seen an empty elevator shaft. Just greasy cables, like giant snakes.

The sight had terrified her, but Daddy had laughed. Indeed, Kit was being silly.

The elevator jerked to a stop, the door opened, and people exited, but this was not their floor. Another stop, the doors opened and people exited, but this was still not their floor. At last, on the eighth floor, Kit’s father nudged her to exit, and so she did, pushing past legs, stepping out of the elevator with two other people, both men, and standing to the side, waiting for her father to join her, but where was Daddy? The elevator door was closing, and Daddy was still inside!

Kit stood staring, incredulous. Her mouth was slack with wonder at how the elevator door had just closed .

It had been one of Kit’s worries, for as long as she could remember, that in a strange place like this she would become separated from her mother: at the grocery store, with many aisles and people pushing shopping carts, or in Macy’s at the mall, or on an escalator that was moving, where, if you stepped onto one of the stairs, you could not step back down but had to go up.

It had not happened yet to Kit that she had been separated from her mother, but, still, her mother seemed to have been separated from her .

And now it was Daddy that Kit worried about being separated from. Daddy is just hiding, to make me laugh , she thought.

Daddy did like to make Kit laugh, and Daddy did like to tease. But Daddy could not now see Kit or laugh at her for being silly.

It was not possible that Daddy had stepped out of the elevator just behind her, because Kit would have seen him if he had. Kit would be seeing him now, and she did not see him.

Too frightened, too stunned to call, Daddy ? Daddy ? Her voice was such a sad, weak voice, no one would hear.

What to do? Where to go? She was just standing there by the elevator. Her heart beating as fast as a sparrow’s heart. Waiting for the elevator door to open—for Kit was sure that it would open, and Daddy would step out laughing at her.

Unless he was annoyed with her. Perhaps Kit had done something wrong unknowingly. Ketchup on the car seat, French fries fallen beneath the seat. A mitten lost. Another mitten lost.

He didn’t like her crying, that was for sure. He would probably tell her, Don’t be a silly baby, just stay where you are. I am on the way.

Trying not to cry. Trying not to shiver so hard. Waiting right in front of the elevator door so Daddy could not miss her. How long it was, how many terrible minutes before the elevator returned, going down. (Kit could see the numbers above the door, an arrow going down from 11 to 10 to 9.) And the door opened, but it must have been a mistake, as no one stepped out. The elevator was full of people, but Daddy was not among them. Daddy did not emerge from the elevator as Kit peered inside frantically. No one noticed her, no one cared in the slightest about her, brooding and inward with their own thoughts, as Daddy sometimes was, and, to her horror, the elevator door closed again.

But where was Daddy?

All this had to be a mistake: Daddy knew that Kit was on the eighth floor.

Daddy knew and had to be looking for her, so it was important to stay right where she was. If she did not, Daddy would not be able to find her.

Kit was so scared that her teeth were chattering. Her mouth had gone dry—she could not swallow. Could not stop shivering. Breathing in gasps like hiccups, couldn’t draw enough breath, so it felt as if she were drowning because she was so, so cold .

Abruptly, Katherine’s voice breaks off. She is very pale, seems to be having difficulty breathing even now. She lifts a water glass to her mouth, but a fit of coughing overcomes her. Water spills down her hand and onto the enamel tabletop.

Katherine? Are you all right?

I am anxious for my friend, who may be hyperventilating. But, when I reach for her hand, Katherine jerks away and, with a weak smile, signals that she is all right and I shouldn’t make a fuss.

Katherine’s eyes are shadowed; her usually smooth forehead is creased. Her hand holding the water glass is trembling. She is embarrassed and apologetic—vexed with herself for having lost control in this public place. It is so unlike Katherine Carpenter, who is normally poised, restrained. Not one to talk at length—and rarely about herself—but today she has been telling me her chilling story in a halting voice, as if she were groping in the dark. Though it is obviously a personal story, she tells it as if the child, Kit, were a stranger, a figure to be pitied.

Katherine rises unsteadily from the table. Excuses herself to go to the rest room. So sorry! I’ll be right back.

Left alone at our table, I am feeling awkward, self-conscious. Usually at the Purple Onion, a moderately priced café, we are a group, never fewer than four friends; always at one of the café’s round tables, which we book in advance.

The restaurant is nearly deserted, as it is early, only a few minutes past noon. The story that Katherine has been telling is painful to hear. I’m dreading what comes next.

Shortly after eight this morning, Katherine called to ask if we could meet for lunch. It was late notice, but there was such urgency in her voice that I hardly recognized it.

Our lunches at the Purple Onion are often lively, festive. The laughter of women together, without men. Divorcées, widows. When the ex-husband dies, the divorcée becomes an honorary widow. At another lunch, we’d welcomed Katherine to this status, amid much laughter.

Today feels odd, just Katherine and me. As if the world has shrunk.

Jerry Hsu captures the city’s manic extremes, with photographs of overturned cars, collisions, and a bank building ablaze.

Jerry Hsu grew up in San Jose, about an hour south of San Francisco, and, for a time, he assumed he would never leave. He didn’t need to. In the late nineties and two-thousands, Hsu and his daredevil friends had proudly put their sleepy Silicon Valley city on the map as an unlikely skateboarding capital. He noticed that young skateboarders from around the country were moving to San Jose, “and it had to do with my group of friends and these videos we were making,” he told me. “It’s like when a random city becomes very important for some random reason. We were able to have our slice of heaven.”

The son of Taiwanese immigrants, Hsu was a precocious talent and became a professional skateboarder in his mid-teens. Magazines sent photographers to San Jose to shoot pictures of him, and he eventually became interested in their craft, what kind of gear they were using, the parallels between their respective art forms. His mother would drive him to the local Barnes & Noble, where he grew fascinated with how Nan Goldin and Larry Clark chronicled the micro-scenes around them. (She also famously procured him a concrete parking block so that he could practice tricks at home.) As skateboard companies sent him around the world in his late teens and twenties, he began obsessively taking photographs of the strange, funny, often macabre things he came across, and publishing them on Tumblr or in Vice magazine.

In 2011, Hsu moved to Los Angeles, primarily for a relationship, and to further his career as a skateboarder. But he also felt a private excitement about spending time photographing a city “that was more rich with things I wanted to see.” With a body thrashed by occupational hazards, Hsu, who is forty-four, orients his life nowadays around running Sci-Fi Fantasy, his skate company, and roaming the city to take pictures. His latest book, “ How About Never ,” is a brutal and wondrous chronicle of the sights he has sought out these past fifteen years.

It’s no surprise that a skateboarder, constantly scanning the landscape for surfaces to recontextualize, might see the world differently. Hsu’s photographs explore the city’s manic extremes. Some of them are quick visual gags: the symmetry of two discarded toilets stacked like yin and yang (or in a sixty-nine position) on the side of the street, a veiny sex toy that’s washed up in a brackish puddle. A triangular slab has fallen neatly out of a wall, as though it was too weary to go on. He notices signs of life where others might just perceive neglect, such as a flower bush sequestered behind a foreboding fence. One picture feels like a short story waiting to be written: a tree hollowed out by rot has been stuffed with roses by a neighbor who felt sorry for it. Hsu maps a Los Angeles of leftovers and castoffs; portraits of friends and strangers in the street are full of dazed, inscrutable expressions.

“My attraction to risk is ever present,” he explains. Hsu is the type of person who runs toward fire, as evidenced by pictures of overturned cars, collisions, a bank building ablaze. They manage to avoid feeling grimly voyeuristic. Instead, there’s a sense of stillness in these images, akin to that flash of calm after you’ve done something ruinous to your body but before your brain registers pain or begins cycling through consequences. I was drawn to a picture of a smashed car windshield, the glass frozen in a series of circular ripples, until it began to resemble the vertical slit of a reptilian eye. It was still in mind a few pages later, as I studied how a young man’s artificial eye seemed to match the orange shade of his hoodie.

My favorite picture in the book finds a sensibly blue Subaru station wagon that has somehow turned on its side in the middle of the night. There’s something funny about its vanity license plate (“ 4A POEM ”) and the way the car’s headlights shine brightly on a house in the distance, as if to point attention away from itself.

Hsu says that his ex-wife often remarked that he had a sixth sense for stumbling upon bizarre, uncanny scenes. Many of his images, even the faintly violent ones, possess an absurdist humor: in one, a motorist explains to a police officer why their Toyota has hopped the curb, but, from a distance, it almost looks like the sedan is playfully trying to return to its mates in a used-car lot. Hsu explained that he finds a lot of his subjects by using Citizen , the incident-reporting app, to see if anything intriguing is happening nearby.

For all the book’s darkness, there are pictures that feel sublime and vast. There are numerous pictures from the hills surrounding Los Angeles where you can’t tell whether the city is on fire or merely aglow with energy. A suburban home like any other sits haloed by clouds, with California’s placid skies a screen of infinite possibility. A picture of a cat vaulting from a gate to a fence takes on an outsized feeling of hope. “Maybe this is corny,” Hsu explained to me, “but all this chaos and these little beautiful secrets I found here reminded me of myself. It was a mirror and threshold.”

I first learned about Hsu in the early two-thousands. My younger cousin wound up skating at his house a few times and excitedly asked if we were related to him. Sadly, the answer was no. Admiring Hsu’s twin careers taught me to see my own Silicon Valley suburb differently, even though I was someone who’d felt the urge to leave as soon as I could. I realized that I hadn’t tried hard enough to appreciate all the beauty and weirdness that was actually available to me.

Where Hsu’s early work was filled with the people in his life, his work over the past decade is marked by a kind of solitude. Some of “How About Never” feels uncomfortably intimate, from its opening image of a cake flower resting on a knife above a dingy sink to pictures of hospital rooms, scabs and bruises, his ex-wife resting her palms on the sink in their bathroom. Hsu says that he spent nearly ten years editing the book, and that he recently realized that it also tracks the dissolution of his marriage. As he put it, there’s a private story of “hope, despair, all the feelings that are associated with trying to make a loving relationship happen” in how the images are sequenced.

Hsu spoke to me from his home in Los Angeles, and at one point, he angled his laptop to show me a shelf full of negatives and contact sheets, and hard drives of digital photos. His archives contain nearly every picture he’s taken in the past twenty-five years, even random things he texts to his friends. He rarely deletes pictures from his phone, thinking that even the imperfect shots might be meaningful to him someday. It reminded me of the famous series of home movies that Hsu made of himself, as a teen-ager, practicing tricks in his parents’ garage. The result of all those hours of practice was a style of effortless cool. Yet he felt compelled to keep a record of all the failures and misses along the way. “Maybe because I have this type of vision, it really takes away from another type that’s more practical,” he said, laughing. A few minutes after we hung up, he got an alert on his phone: a car had just flipped over in Koreatown. ♦

By Shalom Auslander September 14, 2026 Will these pants still fit me? 100% No.

Is it my fault? 100% Yes.

I don’t mean the pants—I mean everything. 100% Yes.

It’s a beautiful day, with bright-blue skies, a warm sun, and a cool breeze. So this afternoon I’m going to take a walk in the park. I will pass a young couple in love, laughing in the sunshine. Will I assume that they are laughing at me? 100% Yes.

Spot on my neck: Cancer? 88% Yes. 12% More tests are needed, none of which my insurance will cover.

I’ve forgotten where I parked—am I getting old? 10% Yes. 90% I am getting old, but in this case my car has been stolen.

At some point during today’s session, will it seem to me that my shrink is writing a lot more on his notepad than usual? 100% Yes.

Is he? 100% Yes.

Approximately how long after I receive my scalding-hot coffee will the turbulence begin? 10% Immediately. 20% As the flight attendant is handing it over, just above my laptop. 70% It doesn’t matter—the engines have all failed.

Just going back to that spot on my neck: Is a spot with defined edges cancer, or a spot with undefined edges? 100% Whichever kind of spot I have is cancer.

I read a novel recently that was legitimately awful. Even putting aside the dull structure and thin characters, it was clear that the writer had nothing new to say and couldn’t even be bothered to risk saying an old thing in a new way; the entire book felt like an exercise in cynicism, as if it had been crafted with the sole intention of being just middling enough to succeed. Will it be a best-seller? 50% National best-seller. 50% Global phenomenon.

Will it win awards? 100% Yes.

Will the awards be given on merit or just to annoy me personally? 100% Just to annoy me personally.

Why is that car following me? It’s been following me for, like, fifteen minutes. 10% Because he’s behind me on the 405. 90% Because he’s following me home to kill me.

What was that noise? 100% Something bad.

After a casual lunch with a good friend, will I, later, overthinking the conversation, take a few of her words out of context and interpret them as a vicious attack? 100% Yes.

Will I know, before she and I get together again, that I will perceive an attack regardless of what she says? 100% Yes.

And will I perceive it anyway? 100% Yes.

Remember that thing I did, a few weeks back, that everyone said I shouldn’t do, but which I did anyway, because I march to the beat of my own drum and because fortune favors the brave? Will that blow up in my face? 40% Yes. 30% It already has. 30% “Blow up” doesn’t quite cover it.

Does anyone else hear that humming sound? 100% No.

Back to that spot on my neck: Treatable? 100% No. But, even if it is, my undiscovered brain tumor is not.

Comedy or tragedy? Too close to call. ♦
